explanations.explanation: King Agrippa tells him, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” That's the green light. Paul is the one who gets to speak, friend.

Agrippa says nothing about witnesses. His words are, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Paul does bring up people who could testify, but only in passing. He says the Jews can testify to how he lived “…if they are willing…” (Acts 26:5).
That's not what the king offers. Agrippa says, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” So Paul isn't cross-examining anybody. He's making his own defense.
Right on the money. Agrippa gives permission, then Paul stretches out his hand and begins his defense. He's about to speak for himself, and he starts with his hand stretched out.
The text says the opposite. Once Agrippa gives permission, “…Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense…” So the hand goes out and the defense begins.

explanations.answer: The king knows Jewish customs well
explanations.explanation: Paul says it plainly: “…you are acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies.” The charges come from the Jews, so a king who knows those customs can follow what Paul is talking about. It's like explaining a work mix-up to a coworker who already knows how your office runs.

explanations.answer: The king owes Paul a favor
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything about a favor. His reason is that the king is “…acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies.” Paul isn't calling in a debt. He's glad for a listener who knows the subject.

explanations.answer: The king has already freed him once
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says Agrippa freed Paul before. Paul's reason is that the king knows “…all the Jewish customs and controversies.” The only talk of release comes at the very end, when Agrippa says Paul could have been released if he had not appealed (Acts 26:32).
That's the word. Paul says he “…lived as a Pharisee, adhering to the strictest sect of our religion.” He says the same thing about himself in Philippians 3:5. If anyone knew the rulebook, it was him.

Not the one Paul names. The Sadducees say there is no resurrection (Acts 23:8). Paul is about to ask why anyone would find it incredible that God raises the dead, so he's clearly not speaking as one of them.
Paul doesn't use that word here. He says he lived as a Pharisee, “…adhering to the strictest sect of our religion.” That's his résumé, and he reads it plainly.

explanations.answer: His hope in God's promise to their fathers
explanations.explanation: Paul says, “…I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers…” He adds that the twelve tribes are hoping to see that promise fulfilled as they serve God day and night. So the charge, in Paul's telling, comes down to hope.

explanations.answer: His teaching against the temple in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That's not how Paul puts it here. He says he's on trial “…because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers…” The temple does come up later, but only as the place where the Jews seized him (Acts 26:21).

explanations.answer: His refusal to honor the laws of Rome
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing like that in this speech. He says, “…I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers…” That's how he states the charge.
Paul asks, “Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” Notice the words “…any of you…” That's a bold way to put a question.
Judging is a big Bible theme, but it's not Paul's word here. He asks, “Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” The question is about God raising the dead.

Remembering is a sweet verb, friend, but it isn't the one Paul uses. He asks, “Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” Notice he doesn't just state it. He asks it, and he hands the room the hard part. A verse earlier he was speaking to “O king,” and now he says “…any of you…”

He says it himself: “…I put many of the saints in prison, and when they were condemned to death, I cast my vote against them.” That was with authority from the chief priests. Paul isn't hiding any of it, and I respect that.

Paul says it was true, and he says it out loud. He tells them, “…I put many of the saints in prison…” and that he cast his vote against them when they were condemned to death. He's owning his past in front of a king.

The voice says, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” Saul was going after the saints, and the voice says it's Him he's persecuting. I think hearing my own name called twice from heaven would stop me in my tracks.

explanations.answer: Why do you run from Me
explanations.explanation: That's not the question. Paul was on his way to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. The voice asks, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?”
The voice doesn't ask about doubt. It asks, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” The question is about what Saul was doing, not what he was thinking.

Paul asks, “Who are You, Lord?” and the answer comes: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting…” Paul had been working against the name of Jesus of Nazareth, and now he hears that name from the Lord Himself. That's a real turning point for him.
Not Elijah, the prophet of Israel (1 Kings 18:36). The Lord answers, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting…” That answer gives Paul his answer straight.

Gabriel is an angel who stands in the presence of God (Luke 1:19), but that's not who answers. The Lord says, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting…” Paul gets a name, and it's the one he'd been opposing.

Jesus says, “…I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and as a witness of what you have seen from Me and what I will show you.” A witness tells what he has seen. So Saul gets sent out with something real to report.
Not a judge. Jesus appoints Saul “…as a servant and as a witness of what you have seen from Me and what I will show you.” A judge sits and decides, but a witness goes and tells.

Priest isn't the word Jesus uses. He says Saul is appointed “…as a servant and as a witness…” Saul had been traveling with the authority and commission of the chief priests, but this job comes from Jesus.
Jesus says they may receive “…forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.” So forgiveness and an inheritance sit together in one sentence. That's two gifts, friend.

A new name sounds lovely, friend, but Jesus doesn't list it here. He says they may receive “…forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.” Notice the order: eyes opened, a turn from darkness to light, and then the forgiveness and the inheritance. I'd say that's already a full box.

A long life would be nice, friend, and I'd happily take some extra years myself. But Jesus doesn't mention it in this line. He says they receive “…forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.” Notice that the inheritance comes among others, with everyone who is sanctified by faith in Him.
The text says the opposite. Paul declared that people should repent and turn to God, “…performing deeds worthy of their repentance.” So what they do is supposed to show it.
Right, it's false. Paul says he declared that they should “…repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance.” So repentance was meant to show up in what people do.

explanations.answer: He would suffer and rise first from the dead
explanations.explanation: Paul says the prophets and Moses said “…that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.” So suffering and rising are both in the plan. Paul says he's adding nothing beyond what they said.

explanations.answer: He would conquer Rome with a mighty army
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about an army or about Rome. He says the Christ would suffer and be the first to rise from the dead. Paul stays with what the prophets and Moses said would happen.

explanations.answer: He would rule forever without ever suffering
explanations.explanation: Paul puts suffering right up front. He says the prophets and Moses said “…that the Christ would suffer…” After that comes the rising from the dead, so suffering isn't skipped.
Paul says the light goes to more than one group. The Christ “…would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.” Gentiles are the non-Jewish nations, so the light isn't kept inside one people.
False it is. Paul says the Christ would “…proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.” The Gentiles, the non-Jewish nations, are named right there. Israel gets the light, and so do they.

Festus, the governor, shouts, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” He blames the learning, not the chains or the road. That's a strange compliment dressed up as an insult.
Festus doesn't blame prison. The governor shouts, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” His target is Paul's learning.

Journeys aren't what Festus names, friend. He exclaims in a loud voice, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” The blame lands on Paul's learning. Then Paul answers, “I am not insane, most excellent Festus; I am speaking words of truth and sobriety.”
Paul says the opposite. He tells Agrippa, “I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner.” So Paul is confident the king has not missed these things.

Right, the statement is false. Paul says, “I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner.” So he says the very opposite of a hidden corner. In his words, these events were not done in a corner.

explanations.answer: He asks if Paul can persuade him to become a Christian that fast
explanations.explanation: Agrippa asks, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” Paul had just said, “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.” I think that question hit close, but the text doesn't tell us what was in Agrippa's heart.

explanations.answer: He says he gave up on the prophets long ago
explanations.explanation: Agrippa doesn't say that. Paul asks, “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.” The king answers with a question about becoming a Christian in such a short time (Acts 26:28). Nothing in the text says he gave up on anything.

explanations.answer: He tells the guards to take Paul away right now
explanations.explanation: No guards get called here. Agrippa asks, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” Later the king and governor simply rise to leave (Acts 26:30).

explanations.answer: That they would all become what he is
explanations.explanation: Paul says, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.” He's wishing for the king AND everyone listening. He doesn't wish for the chains, friend, and who could blame him?

explanations.answer: That they would all set him free today
explanations.explanation: Paul's wish isn't about his freedom. He says, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.” He's wishing something for them, not asking something from them.

explanations.answer: That they would all judge him fairly
explanations.explanation: That's not his wish, friend. Paul says, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am…” He wishes it for all who hear him, not only the king. The only part he leaves out is “…except for these chains.”
They said the opposite. On the way out, they tell one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.” That's a pretty good review of Paul from the people who just heard him.

Correct. On their way out, the king and the others say to one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.” So the statement is false, because they say the opposite. Imprisonment is right there in what they say he has not done anything worthy of.

Agrippa tells Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.” Paul had made that appeal himself earlier (Acts 25:11). So the appeal to Caesar is the very thing Agrippa names.
Felix was the governor before Festus (Acts 24:27). But Agrippa says Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. Caesar is the one named.

Pontius Pilate was the governor who handed Jesus over to be crucified (Matthew 27:2, 26). He isn't in this scene at all. Agrippa says Paul “…could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
